title: [B2 • Band 6.0] Bài 203: The Revival of Acoustic Ecology
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 203 (LEVEL B2 • BAND 6.0)

The Revival of Acoustic Ecology

Paragraph A. For decades, conservation biology relied heavily on visual surveys. Ecologists set up camera traps, walked through dense undergrowth with binoculars, or flew drones above tree canopies to count wildlife. Yet visual methods face obvious limits: animals hide among leaves, avoid human smell, or emerge only in total darkness. In response, soundscape ecology is changing how scientists judge environmental health. By listening to an entire habitat's audio signature—from chirping crickets to booming howler monkeys—researchers gain a clearer picture of ecosystem balance than sightings alone can offer.

Paragraph B. Acoustic ecologists divide environmental audio into three main categories: biophony (sounds from non-human living creatures), geophony (natural non-living sounds like rainfall, thunder, and wind), and anthrophony (human mechanical noise). In undisturbed ecosystems, biophony follows Dr. Bernie Krause's 'acoustic niche hypothesis': over millions of years, diverse species evolved to vocalize in specific frequency bands and time slots so their mating and warning calls do not overlap or drown each other out. When logging fragments a rainforest, this natural acoustic structure breaks down, leaving the habitat quiet and disjointed.

Paragraph C. The technological driver behind this shift is the autonomous recording unit (ARU). These inexpensive, weatherproof devices are strapped to tree trunks to record ambient sound continuously for months. However, early teams were quickly buried under massive audio archives: twelve ARUs in one reserve can collect thirty thousand hours of recordings in a single season, requiring decades of human labour to listen through manually. Consequently, acoustic ecology remained limited until machine learning algorithms became capable of scanning large audio datasets automatically.

Paragraph D. To automate analysis, Dr. Julian Rivera created an algorithmic platform named SoundID. Rather than identifying every individual species, the software calculates mathematical indices showing how acoustic energy is spread across multiple frequency bands. In field trials across forty forest plots in Peru, Rivera found that areas damaged by illegal selective logging—which satellite surveys often failed to detect beneath the dense forest roof—showed sharp drops in acoustic diversity scores within forty-eight hours of timber removal.

Paragraph E. Despite these advances, field practitioners still battle tough physical obstacles. High tropical humidity and fungal spores corrode delicate microphone membranes, forcing frequent maintenance. Intense monsoon downpours also create loud geophonic noise that masks high-pitched animal calls for days. Meanwhile, near urban roads, low-frequency engine vibrations from highway traffic can overwhelm automated detectors, leading algorithms to falsely register empty forests.

Paragraph F. Even so, acoustic monitoring proves invaluable for measuring ecological restoration. In former farmland in Costa Rica, replanted forests looked visually mature within seven years, yet their acoustic diversity remained poor for nearly two decades until fallen logs and layered bushes returned to support specialist birds and insects. As Dr. Bernie Krause notes, a photograph captures only a frozen moment in space, whereas a soundscape tells the living story of an entire ecosystem across time.

groups.title: Questions 5–6
groups.instructions:
Choose TWO letters, A–E.
Which TWO problems regarding autonomous recording units (ARUs) are mentioned in the text?
options: A. They are too expensive for small research teams to purchase.
B. They generate far more audio data than humans can review manually.
C. Their wireless signals are blocked by thick jungle leaves.
D. Their delicate microphone parts suffer damage in humid tropical forests.
E. They are frequently destroyed by wild animals in reserves.
